The Court also gave these schools the option of switching to Kannada or the child's mother tongue as the medium of instruction from class I to stay in line with the law.

Heading: Vigilance to probe corruption charges against CPI(M) leaders - Indian Express
Content:
The Electronics Corporation of Tamil Nadu (ELCOT) has come up with a novel idea to test the durability of laptop computers — it makes people walk on finished products.

ELCOT, the nodal agency for Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) projects for the state Government, developed the concept named 'Fire Walk' to ensure the ruggedness of the laptops.

"People weighing 85 to 92 kg are asked to walk on the laptops placed on the floor. Only then do we issue a clearance certificate," said an official.

Post fire walk, the machines are tested for their performance, and the vendor gets a clearance to participate in the price bid only if the system functions smoothly. To assure transparency of testing procedure, a video of fire walking is featured on Youtube, a popular social networking and video-sharing site.

According to senior officials, this test was incorporated to ensure that the laptop, a supposedly sophis- ticated and fragile equipment, could withstand tough conditions and handling.

"We have already completed testing the first lot of 500 laptops that we had ordered. The fire walk test would be conducted on almost all the laptops as an on going process," said the official in charge of the project. He assured that the machines given to students can withstand almost any shock.

Other tests include a technical assessment of the machine to make sure that the computer is fully compatible with different versions of Linux operating system. The agency had launched an ambitious project to provide laptop computers to 1,00,000 students at reduced rates.

"The computers come with a three-year international warranty except for the battery, hence the students who travel abroad after completing their studies in India will have no difficulty in getting warranty services wherever they go," the ELCOT website informed.

ELCOT had announced that it would provide branded laptops at a reduced rate of Rs 31,717 to one lakh students from the LKG level to students of professional colleges.

Heading: Relocated Sariska tiger likely to be released soon - Indian Express
Content:
Dealing a severe blow to the CPI(M) state leadership, Enquiry Commissioner and Special Judge (Vigilance) S Jagadeesh on Wednesday asked the state vigilance and anti-corruption bureau to initiate fresh investigations into the scams involving party mouthpiece Deshabhimani.

Jagadeesh asked the vigilance police to re-open the Rs 2-crore bribery case that involved Deshabhimani general manager and CPM central committee member E P Jayarajan and another corruption case against its deputy general manager P Venugopal.

While, Jayarajan allegedly accepted a Rs 2 crore bribe from lottery king Santiago Martin, wanted in Kerala for evading tax worth several crores, Venugopal had taken Rs 1-crore from LiS, a fraudulent money chain in Kerala.

Venugopal had received the money, as the first installment of an alleged Rs 3-crore deal, to influence a probe into the irregularities of LiS. The company was facing charges of cheating the public and flouting RBI regulations.

However, the police failed to collect evidence to substantiate the corruption charges against Jayarajan and Venugopal after the Vigilance court directed the police to probe the issue last year. The court ordered a probe following a petition by Advocate P Rahim, of Indian Lawyers Congress, alleging a corrupt liaison between Martin and the CPM.

Rejecting the earlier report, the court said the investigation report was incomplete. "In the case involving Jayarajan, the police did not record the statements of witnesses produced by the plaintiff. Even Santiago Martin had claimed that he had given money to Deshabhimani as bond," the court said.

With regard to the LiS bribery case, the court said the police had failed to examine the accounts of the financial institution and should also have taken into consideration that Venugopal was sacked from Deshabhimani for corruption charges.

The CPM initially claimed the money from Martin was taken as a bond, but contradicted its own statement saying the amount was an advance for advertisement costs. The U-turn came after the party consulted legal experts and realised that Deshabhimani could not have legally floated bonds.

Heading: Left ties suffer as CPI leader arrested - Indian Express
Content:
The tiger is back in Sariska.

Days after making his first kill, the tiger has been showing signs if establishing his territory. "The young male translocated from Ranthambore is making sounds typical of those that mark a territory. This is a good sign and will help us release it soon," said Wildlife Institute of India Director P R Sinha.

The herbivores out there in the open, beyond the enclosure where the tiger is housed at present, have felt the big cat's presence and have been making "tiger alarm calls" to warn each other. "It seems that the tiger has been able to leave its mark. The herbivores in the forest can feel that the jungle's largest predator has returned and have started making alarm calls to each other. The progress graph has been amazing and it indicates that we can release him soon," said Sinha.

The WII scientists who have been tracking the young tigress that would be translocated from Ranthambore to Sariska next, said that it is also active. "Like her male partner, she too made a kill on Monday. We will translocate her soon provided the clear weather holds," Sinha told The Indian Express.

According to experts, the results of the absence of the big cat in the tiger reserve are showing. "The tiger is an umbrella specie and best indicates the health of the forest. Its absence for the past two years has had definite effects on the surroundings. The leopards and the herbivorous population have gone up and that has led to over grazing in the forest," an official said.

Although the number of leopards have increased, they have not been able to keep the large ungulate population found in this traditional tiger habitat in check. A good habitat in the tiger reserve is now a problem as the Nilgai and Sambar population has gone up manifolds. The resident cattle population around the reserve forest has also increased leading to overgrazing of the forest.

Heading: Junk food may hit health of unborn child: study - Indian Express
Content:
Following the arrest of P S Supal, state secretary of the CPI's youth wing, AIYF, on Wednesday the relation between the Left coalition partners in Kerala — the CPI(M) and the CPI — hit a new low.

Supal, who was picked up by the CPI(M)-controlled state police officials in the wee hours, was charged with forcefully releasing CPI workers, who were arrested for rioting during a co-operative bank election at Edaman, in Kollam district on June 28.

The former MLA was produced before a magistrate court, which remanded him to judicial custody for 15 days. He was later released on bail. Following the arrest, CPI members observed a hartal in several areas of Kollam district. AIYF activists took out a march to the state secretariat, to protest against the police action.

CPI Kollam district secretary K Prakashbabu told The Indian Express that police would not have dared to arrest Supal without the support of the CPI(M) district leadership. He said his party would seek action against police officials in Kollam district.

The stand-off between the Left parties in Kollam was set off after a CPI(M) member won the chairmanship of the district co-operative bank. Unable to bear the humiliation, the CPI quit as the convener of the LDF in the district. Later, the party nominee quit as deputy mayor in Kollam.

Heading: Chandu Padhiyar’s only fault: he availed loan before March 1997 - Indian Express
Content:
If you are pregnant and have been indulging your cravings for junk food, stop right now. Greasy, fatty foods could affect your unborn child and may lead to long-lasting and irreversible damage from heart disease to diabetes, says new research published in the Journal of Physiology.

The study was conducted at the Royal Veterinary College, London where the experts fed female rats—which share a number of fundamental biological systems with humans—a junk-food diet of crisps, cheese, muffins and other processed foods throughout pregnancy and lactation.

It was seen that the frequent intake of such food sent insulin and glucose in the blood to unusually high rates, which is the most common cause of Type-2 diabetes. Also, children who were overweight at birth were born with a taste for junk food themselves.

Dr Anoop Misra Director and head, Department of Diabetes and Metabolic Diseases, Fortis Hospital says, "Some chemicals from the feeding centre could be sensitising the brain of the unborn foetus towards junk food."

Even when the babies were fed with a healthy diet, says the study, medical problems continued . "Junk-food babies had a host of medical problems that lasted beyond adolescence into adulthood," says the study.

The study showed that the rats had increased cholesterol and triglyceride levels - both linked to heart disease.

The rats also remained significantly podgier than normal with extra fat around the kidneys, another diabetes risk factor.

While, the ill-effects were monitored in both the sexes, researchers found that the female offsprings were particularly affected, with high levels of glucose and the appetite-promoting hormone leptin making them prone to obesity.

Doctors insist that it is very important for pregnant women to eat a healthy diet.

"If the mother eats an excessive amount of sugary or fatty food, her lipid profile, sugar levels will be deranged. This is transmitted to the baby and when the child grows up it will also develop the same problems. It is therefore very important for the mother to eat a protein-rich diet and lot of milk products," said Dr Anuradha Kapur, senior consultant, Obstetrics and Gynaecology, in Delhi's Max Super Specialty Hospital.

Heading: It’s better to be a defaulter, sulks Purshottam Das - Indian Express
Content:
The Vivid Karyaki Cooperative Union Ltd (VIKA) office in Miyagam is witnessing an unprecedented rush these days, as farmers mill around the notice board eagerly to check if their names figure on the lone-waiver list.

One farmer who got 'lucky' is Punja Padhiyar, 47. Relieved of Rs 2,64,366 debt, he says the waiver was a new lease of life. "We couldn't have even dreamt of being relieved of the debt if this waiver had not come from the Prime Minister. He saved us." Punja, who lives with his three unmarried sons and his wife in Jariwalu Faliyu said, "I have decided not to fall into debt again. We will buy a few more cattle and earn a better living."

But for those who took loans before March 31, 1997, the picture remains bleak. Chandu Padhiyar, 62, did not qualify for any waiver for this very reason. He is now filled with despair having lost 1.75 of his 8 acres after the Narmada canal passed through his field. "Now my farm remains submerged for six months, and with only one crop a year, life has become impossible," he says. "We borrowed Rs 37,500 over the entire piece of land but the Central Government has a stifling waiver rider. My total debt is Rs 81,617 and I have given up hope of repaying it. Now we are sowing crops by borrowing from people but it's an endless circle that is killing us slowly."

Heading: Gulzar can’t thank Govt enough - Indian Express
Content:
Even as hordes of farmers are celebrating the implementation of the agricultural debt waiver scheme in the state, Purshottam Das, a farmer from Barwala, is cursing the Government for not extending the benefits to law-abiding citizens like him.

"Tell me why am I not a beneficiary of the loan waiver scheme? Is it my fault that I have been repaying the instalments on the Rs 45,000 loan that I took on May 30, 2007? Is it my fault to be honest? Why should I not get any benefit of the waiver while those who did not care to repay the loan have been bailed out?" he asks, still finding it very difficult to understand why his name does not figure in the name of the beneficiaries.

"What justice is this and what is the message the Government wants to give to the farmers," questions Purshottam Das.

Das says having learnt his lesson now, he will be more careful next time he takes a loan. "I will make sure I don't repay the loan. After all, it pays to be a defaulter rather than paying back instalments on time," he says.

The bank and credit society officials, too, are a worried lot. "Many farmers who were defaulters earlier are now eligible for fresh loans, after their dues being waived off. We fear they won't pay the instalments in future as well," says Gaman Arora, manager, State Bank of India, Barwala branch.

Heading: ‘The Congress has blessed me’ - Indian Express
Content:
Gulzar Singh Virk, a resident of village Alipur Araian near Patiala, will benefit a total of Rs 2,86,700 from the Centre's 71,000-crore loan waiver scheme.

Gulzar, who owns four acres of land, had taken Rs 1 lakh as crop loan and another Rs 3.5 lakh under the Kisan Gold Card loan for buying a tractor and for sowing seeds.

Though he is yet to receive a certificate of loan waiver under the scheme from the State Bank of Patiala's Agriculture Development Branch, from where he had availed the loan on November 22, 2005, an elated Gulzar says, "I am very happy over this development and am thankful to the Government for bringing me out of my loan crisis."

Gulzar, who lost his father and brother in separate incidents, says the loan waiver has come as a welcome relief after many years.

Still recuperating from an accident he suffered last month, Gulzar says he has to take care of a big family, including his mother and his brother's family, besides his own.

"I will never forget this favour done to me and my family," adds Gulzar.

Heading: Some got really lucky, others rued - Indian Express
Content:
For Bitana, 60, of Chaudharypurwa village in Barabanki district, June 30 was one of the happiest days of her life. As the chief general manager of SBI distributed loan waiver certificates to some 486 small farmers out of 3,000 from the district in the first lot, Bitana was one of four beneficiaries from her village. A year ago, she had taken a loan of Rs 12,000, which became Rs 13,748 with interest, to buy seeds and fertilizer, but a poor yield made her unable to repay the money. The waiver, however, lightened her burden. "The Congress has blessed me," she says, echoing the new-found allegiance that beneficiaries such as her have towards the Congress, even though the MLA in this area is from the ruling BSP and the MP from the BJP.

However, others have been less fortunate. Rammurat, also of Chaudharypurwa, took a loan of Rs 10,000 on his kisan credit card, but did not feature on the first list released by the State Bank of India. "I have only 4 beeghas of land and I did not have a good crop. If my loan is not waived, I may not be able to sow my field," he said, adding that he is investing his hopes on the bank's second list, expected to come out next week.

Heading: Resentment simmers over 5-acre clause - Indian Express
Content:
The loan waiver came too late for 55-yr-old Raghunath Tukaram Rajapure from Chambli village, Purandar taluka. Both his sons have already dropped out of school. Rajapure took a loan of Rs 30,000 in 2003, of which he could pay back only Rs 14,000. The remaining Rs 16,000 has been waived off.

"My younger son left school after completing Class IX, while my elder son gave up his plans to go for higher education after clearing Class XII. Both my sons have now moved to Pune to run sugarcane juice centres," Rajapure told The Indian Express.

"The loan waiver has taken away my burden of repayment of loan, but I do not think farming alone would help me meet the daily needs of my household," he added.

The list of beneficiaries declared on Tuesday in Pune villages ended days of anxiousness for farmers who were not sure if their names would feature in it.

Pandurang Namdeo Shendkar (76) of Chambli village could not believe his ears when the news of his Rs 32,500 loan amount being waived off was given to him. "There was uncertainty over who would feature in the list of beneficiaries. Thankfully, I wasn't left out. The waiver is a big relief for me as I was planning to sell my land to repay the debt," he said.

In Bobgaon, 60-yr-old Ramchandra Somaji Phadtare, who owns 6 acres of land, was unhappy as he was eligible only for partial loan waiver. "I have to repay Rs 50,000, but would get only a partial waiver. I have to start sowing, but I don't have money. I can't even take fresh loan as it would add to the burden of my existing debt." Bhairu Maruti Kamthe is unhappy as his loan of Rs 45,000 would not be completely waived off even though he tills only two acres of land. "Our 6.5 acres of land is registered in the name of my father. Me and my two brothers and do farming separately in approximately 2 acres each. However, I am not eligible for the complete loan waiver as the records show the three fields as a single piece of land."

The loan waiver conditions were most favourable for Laxman Raghunath Kamthe as the 22 acres of land owned by his late father was equally distributed between him and his four siblings. The pending dues of a loan of Rs 2 lakh, too, was thus divided. "Each of us got the responsibility of repayment of Rs 40,000 each," he said, adding that all the five of them got the loan waiver as they had less than five of acre land transferred in their names.

Heading: Only Rs 20,000 waived from Rs 2.30 lakh loan, farmer indifferent - Indian Express
Content:
The loan waiver has generated more bitterness than happiness among the farmers in Surendranagar due to an ironic twist, in which long-term loan defaulters benefit, but not those who have been breaking their backs trying to pay off their debts regularly. Sarji Raisinh a small farmer from Nanikathi village has been lucky. His debt of Rs 40,000— which he had borrowed from Kheti Seva Sahkari Mandali four years ago—has been waived. "I did not have enough money to pay society and I did not," he admits. "While many others borrow from money lenders to pay off banks, I decided not to and that saved me a lot of money. Now many of us will think twice before repaying loans."

A second problem arises from the fact that farmers with more than 5 acres of land do not qualify for the waiver—but this does not take into account that a piece of land registered under the name of one person, usually a father, often gets divided among a number of siblings. Jamal Sapra, a tribal farmer from the same village as Sarji, got the short end of the stick. "We have 11 acres of land registered under my father's name, but since we are three brothers, our per head land holding comes to less than 4 acres. Now with this 5-acre clause, we cannot benefit from the scheme," he says, adding that from now on, he will not be as conscientious about repaying loan—something he did regularly, even borrowing from money lenders. "This has been a common practice here just to keep our credit record clean, but now with this precedence set, many of us will not repay the loan installments any more," he says.
